items.title: Re-shape the prose-anchored extractions in readme-tags.test.js to read structure instead
items.acceptance: The extractions behind T-020 (Attribution counts), T-021 (the --list behaviour section locator) and T-023 (a band heading whose lead-in carries its own "N tags" count) derive their values from document STRUCTURE -- tables, rows, headings-as-headings, tokens -- rather than from a position or literal inside an English sentence, and all three of those items' measured false-rejection cases go green without any of the guards going quiet. items.notes:
Source: cycle-25 standing decision (state.json decisions[], cycle 25) converted into an actionable item at cycle 27, per the cycle-26 handoff's instruction to FILE the re-shape as an M item if it is the right answer but does not fit gear 1. It is, and it does not. WHY AN UMBRELLA RATHER THAN THREE MORE NARROWINGS: every README guard this run built extracts a number by anchoring to a position or a literal in prose, and every fix so far (T-012, T-018, T-020, T-021, T-022, T-023) has narrowed the anchor rather than removed it. The failure direction has been safe every time -- these guards reject a correct README loudly, they never pass a wrong one silently -- but a maintainer's cheapest escape from a false rejection is DELETING the guard, so the cumulative risk is the whole family going at once. A seventh narrowing does not reduce that risk; changing what the extractions read does. HONEST SCOPE NOTE, so this is not mistaken for a bigger claim: T-018 is NOT part of this family and was correctly fixed narrowly at cycle 27 -- its locator was already structural (the `| Tag | Count |` header row plus the separator row) and the defect was an adjacency requirement, not a prose anchor. Band-bound digits (`5+`, `2-4`) are also fine to read from a heading: they carry mathematical meaning, which the cycle-25 finding explicitly permits. The target is prose WORDING as an anchor, nothing else.

items.acceptance: A human rules on two behaviours the Domain rules do not currently decide, and the ruling is written into SPEC.md as an explicit clause either way. (1) --help vs usage-error precedence when both appear in argv: the shipped behaviour is that the usage error WINS in both argv orders (measured: `--help --seed abc` and `--seed abc --help` both exit 2 with "aphorism: flag --seed requires a numeric value" on stderr). (2) Whether `--seed -0` and `--seed 0` are THE SAME SEED: they are `===` in JavaScript, but toUint32Seed folds the IEEE-754 bit pattern including the sign bit, so they select DIFFERENT aphorisms (measured: seed 0 -> Kernighan "most effective debugging tool"; seed -0 -> Saint-Exupery "Perfection is achieved"). Either behaviour is defensible; the SPEC decides neither.
items.notes:
FILED AT CYCLE 4 from J-6, which measured both and correctly declined to pin either with a test. This is a SPEC decision, not a swarm task, and it is filed the way T-040 is: a human ratifies or reverses, and the item is not dispatchable until they do.

WHY NO TEST WAS ADDED, and why that was right: the Domain rules resolve exactly ONE flag-vs-error precedence question explicitly — for --list ("A seed that fails to parse is still a usage error under --list"). The existence of that carve-out is evidence the author does not treat "usage-error trumps other flags" as self-evidently general; where they meant it to generalise, they said so. They never said it for --help. An assertion pinning today s behaviour would therefore be a future false rejection rather than coverage — which is the failure mode J-6 exists to avoid. Same logic for -0/0: the rule guarantees determinism PER SEED VALUE and says nothing about whether -0 and 0 are one value or two.

NOTE FOR WHOEVER RULES ON (2): if the answer is "they are the same seed", that is a PRODUCT bug in toUint32Seed and closing it is a src/ change, which this run s non-goals fence off. If the answer is "they are distinguishable bit patterns, by design", the fix is one SPEC sentence and nothing else. The cheap ruling and the expensive one are not symmetric, so rule before anyone writes code.

HONEST NOTE ON (1) FROM THE BUILDER, disclosed before any gate looked: its "does not map" call on case 1 rests on an INFERENCE from the --list carve-out (silence implies deliberate scoping) rather than on direct textual statement. A reasonable reviewer could read the Exit-codes clause as unconditional and call the current behaviour a hole rather than an unspecified choice. The disagreement is recorded rather than resolved. | CYCLE 4: N-4 added TWO more rulings to this item, both measured. (3) REPEATED --tag/--author (D-42): shipped behaviour is last-occurrence-wins and it is UNPROTECTED - conductor reproduced it independently (--tag humor --tag design --list prints the 14-entry design list; a first-wins mutant prints the 9-entry humor list; the suite stays 102p/0f on both). items.acceptance: bin/aphorism.js registers no error handler on process.stderr, so a closed stderr reader crashes the process and Node’s exit 1 replaces whatever code the run had earned. Fix so that (a) a broken stderr pipe is handled without a raw Node stack trace and without altering the exit code the run earned, and (b) a NON-EPIPE stderr write failure does not silently succeed. CONTROLS that must stay green: with an OPEN stderr reader the usage path still exits 2 and the no-match path still exits 1; stdout behaviour and every exit code on the normal paths are unchanged; the suite still passes.
items.notes: MEASURED by the conductor at cycle 7, not inferred, and independent of the builder that flagged it as out-of-scope. The discriminator is the reader, not the command: `node bin/aphorism.js --bogus-flag 2>&1 >/dev/null | cat >/dev/null` exits 2 (correct) while the identical invocation piped into `true` or `head -0` exits 1. Same command, same arguments, opposite outcome, varying ONLY whether the stderr reader stays open — a theory that this is ordinary argument handling predicts those alike; the unhandled-error theory predicts them opposite, which is what was observed. This is the exit-code collision Q-1 clause (2) removed on stdout, still live on stderr: a script reading exit 1 is told “no aphorism matched” when the truth is “your flag was wrong and the diagnostic could not be delivered”. NOT a descent into the README-prose test family the cycle-0 stress-test decision fenced off, and NOT generated by this cycle’s own fix — it is a pre-existing defect in shipped code that the Q-1 measurement happened to expose.
